title: 22. Interview: Key-Value Stores
summary: Interview Q&A for Key-Value Stores — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Key-Value Stores interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why is a key-value store O(1), and what does that imply for query flexibility?
**Answer:** A key-value store is O(1) because it's literally a hash map — the key is hashed (e.g., MurmurHash3 in Redis, MD5 in Memcached), and the hash determines the bucket/slot in memory (or the shard in a distributed system). Hash map lookups are constant time regardless of dataset size. The implication for query flexibility is severe: you can ONLY query by exact key. "All users older than 30," "all orders between $100-$500," "all sessions created in the last hour" — none of these are native KV operations. To support them, you must build secondary indexes yourself (e.g., a sorted set in Redis keyed by age, or a separate DynamoDB GSI), which means denormalizing at write time and accepting write amplification. The trade-off is fundamental: O(1) requires the access pattern to be known in advance and encoded in the key. Relational databases trade O(1) for O(log N) (B-tree indexes) but gain arbitrary query flexibility. NoSQL key-value stores bet that you'll design keys for your hot access patterns and accept that ad-hoc queries go elsewhere (a search engine, OLAP store, or full-table scan).
**Visual:**
```
KV store (hash map):    key -> hash -> bucket -> value    O(1)

  GET user:42   -> hash(user:42) = 0x5A3F -> bucket 95 -> value
  SET user:42 v -> same hash, write bucket 95

Implication:
  + arbitrary key lookup is sub-ms, regardless of dataset size
  - "WHERE age > 30" is NOT possible without a secondary index
    (build it yourself: ZADD by_age:30 user:42 ...)
  - "JOIN users, orders" is impossible; denormalize at write

RDBMS B-tree:           O(log N) but flexible queries
KV hash map:            O(1) but only key lookup
```

### Q2. What's the difference between Memcached, Redis, and DynamoDB, and when do you choose each?
**Answer:** **Memcached** is a pure in-memory cache: no persistence, no replication, no data structures beyond strings, LRU eviction. Choose it when you want the simplest, fastest possible cache and can tolerate losing everything on restart — typically for caching database query results or rendered pages where the source of truth is elsewhere. ~1M ops/sec per instance, ~50 µs latency. **Redis** is an in-memory data structure store: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets (the killer feature), hashes, streams, hyperloglog, geospatial. It adds optional persistence (RDB snapshots, AOF log), replication, pub/sub, Lua scripting, and Redis Cluster for sharding. Choose Redis when you need rich server-side operations (atomic ZADD for leaderboards, INCR for counters, ZRANGE for top-N), pub/sub, or when the cache must survive restarts. ~100k-500k ops/sec per instance, ~1ms p99. **DynamoDB** is a fully-managed, durable, scaled KV store: Amazon handles partitioning, replication, HA, backups; you pay per request. It adds a sort key (range queries within a partition), secondary indexes (LSI/GSI), and transactions. Choose DynamoDB when you want zero ops, durability, and any scale — accepting per-request cost and a restrictive query model. The decision: pure cache → Memcached; rich data + low latency → Redis; managed + durable → DynamoDB.
**Visual:**
```
              Memcached      Redis          DynamoDB
Speed:        ~1M ops/s      ~100-500k/s    scales (managed)
Persistence:  NO             optional       YES (durable)
Replication:  NO             async          YES (3x automatic)
Data types:   strings        many (ZSET!)   sort key + indexes
Ops burden:   low            medium          zero (managed)
Cost model:   RAM            RAM             per-request
Use case:     pure cache     cache + logic   durable KV at scale

Choose:
  + pure cache, lose-on-restart OK    -> Memcached
  + leaderboards, counters, pub/sub   -> Redis
  + managed, durable, any scale       -> DynamoDB
```

### Q3. Explain the cache-aside pattern and its pitfalls (cache stampede, thundering herd).
**Answer:** Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the most common caching pattern: on read, check the cache first; on miss, read the database, populate the cache, return; on write, invalidate (delete) the cache entry. Benefits: the cache only holds requested data (no wasted space), and a cache failure degrades gracefully (just more DB load). Pitfalls: First, **cache stampede** — when a popular key expires, hundreds of concurrent requests miss simultaneously, all read the DB, all set the cache. The DB gets 100x its normal load for a brief window. Mitigations: probabilistic early expiration (XFetch — refresh the cache slightly before TTL with some probability, spreading the load), request coalescing (only one request goes to the DB, others wait), or per-key locks (Redis SETNX as a mutex). Second, **thundering herd on cold start** — when the cache is empty after a deploy or restart, every request misses. Mitigations: warm the cache before traffic shifts, or use a read-replica DB during warmup. Third, **stale data** — if the DB write doesn't invalidate the cache (write-through and write-behind patterns help), or if invalidation races with reads. Fourth, **cache penetration** — queries for non-existent keys bypass the cache and hit the DB; mitigate by caching negative results (NULL for 60s). Fifth, **cache breakdown** — a single hot key expires, causing stampede on that key.
**Visual:**
```
Cache-aside (lazy load):
  read:  cache.get(key) -> hit? return
                       -> miss? db.read -> cache.set -> return
  write: db.write -> cache.del(key)  (invalidate)

Pitfalls:
  1. STAMPEDE  (popular key expires, 100s miss at once)
     [R1] miss -> DB
     [R2] miss -> DB       <- all hit DB simultaneously
     [R3] miss -> DB
     Fix: XFetch (early refresh) / SETNX lock / request coalescing

  2. COLD START  (cache empty after deploy, all requests miss)
     Fix: warm cache before shifting traffic

  3. STALE  (write to DB, cache not invalidated)
     Fix: write-through (write cache+DB atomically)
            or write-behind (write cache, async to DB)

  4. PENETRATION  (queries for non-existent keys bypass cache)
     Fix: cache NULL for short TTL
```

### Q4. How does Redis achieve atomicity with single-threading, and what are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** Redis uses a single thread for command execution (with I/O threading added in Redis 6 for network reads/writes, but command logic is still serial). Atomicity comes for free: since only one command runs at a time, there's no need for locks, no race conditions, and operations like `INCR`, `ZADD`, `SETNX` are inherently atomic. Lua scripts (via `EVAL`) run atomically as a single unit — perfect for compare-and-set, rate limiting, or multi-step atomic operations. The benefits: deterministic latency (no GC pauses, no lock contention), simple mental model, and 100k+ ops/sec on a single core (commands are O(1) or O(log N) for most ops). The trade-offs: First, **single CPU utilization** — Redis uses one core, so a 32-core machine is wasted; you run multiple Redis instances per box (with separate ports) to use all cores. Second, **long commands block everything** — `KEYS *` on a 10M-key DB blocks the server for seconds; use `SCAN` instead. `SORT` on a huge list, `SUNION` on huge sets — same problem. Third, **no true parallelism within an instance** — if your workload is compute-heavy (Lua scripts doing math), throughput caps at one core. Fourth, **memory bound** — single-instance RAM limits the dataset; for >50GB you need Redis Cluster (sharding across instances). The single-threaded model is a deliberate trade: simplicity and atomicity over parallelism, and it works because KV operations are I/O-bound (network), not CPU-bound.
**Visual:**
```
Redis single-threaded command execution:

  [Net I/O thread 1] -+              +-> [Command thread] -+-> [Net I/O]
  [Net I/O thread 2] -+-> queue ----->   (single core)     |
  [Net I/O thread 3] -+              +---------------------+
                       (Redis 6+)                              -> reply

Atomicity for free:
  INCR counter    -> read counter, +1, write, return  (atomic)
  SETNX lock k v  -> if k absent: set, return 1; else 0  (atomic CAS)
  EVAL "..."      -> whole Lua script runs atomically

Trade-offs:
  + no locks, no races, deterministic latency
  + simple ops are atomic (INCR, ZADD, SETNX)
  - single core (run N instances/box to use all cores)
  - long command blocks (KEYS *, SORT big set) -> use SCAN, SSCAN
  - memory bound (RAM = dataset size + overhead)
```

### Q5. What are Redis sorted sets (ZSETs) and why are they so powerful for leaderboards?
**Answer:** A Redis sorted set (ZSET) is a set where each member has an associated floating-point score, and the set is sorted by score. Operations: `ZADD key score member` adds/updates, `ZREVRANGE key 0 9` returns top 10 by score (highest first), `ZRANK key member` returns the 0-indexed rank, `ZSCORE key member` returns the score, `ZINCRBY key delta member` atomically increments a member's score. Internally, Redis uses a skip list + hash table combo — the hash table gives O(1) member lookup, the skip list gives O(log N) ordered traversal. So `ZADD` is O(log N), `ZRANGE` is O(log N + M) where M = range size, `ZSCORE` is O(1). This is the perfect data structure for leaderboards: a game with 10M players can return the top 10 in microseconds, and a player can learn their rank in microseconds. Real-world: Reddit uses Redis ZSETs for ranking, Stack Overflow for reputation leaderboards, countless games for scoring. Beyond leaderboards, ZSETs power: priority queues (score = priority), sliding-window rate limiting (score = timestamp, range-query the window), delayed job queues (score = execute_at, periodically ZRANGEBYSCORE for due jobs), and time-series indexes (score = timestamp). The combination of atomic server-side operations (ZINCRBY) and efficient ordered traversal is what makes ZSETs uniquely powerful — no other common KV data structure does both.
**Visual:**
```
Redis ZSET (sorted set): member -> score, sorted by score

  ZADD lb 100 alice 95 bob 110 dave 88 carol
        |
        v
  skip list (sorted by score)        hash table (member -> node)
  +-----+----------+                 +-------+-------+
  | 88  | carol    | <-- ZRANK=0    | alice | node  |
  +-----+----------+                 | bob   | node  |
  | 95  | bob      | <-- ZRANK=1    | carol | node  |
  +-----+----------+                 | dave  | node  |
  | 100 | alice    | <-- ZRANK=2    +-------+-------+
  +-----+----------+
  | 110 | dave     | <-- ZRANK=3
  +-----+----------+

  ZREVRANGE lb 0 1 -> [(dave,110), (alice,100)]   top 2
  ZRANK lb alice    -> 2 (or 1 from top? redis is 0=lowest)
  ZINCRBY lb 5 alice-> atomic, alice now 105

Complexity:
  ZADD:        O(log N)
  ZRANGE:      O(log N + M)  (M = result size)
  ZSCORE:      O(1) via hash table
  ZRANK:       O(log N)
  -> 10M-player leaderboard: top-10 in microseconds

Use cases beyond leaderboards:
  + priority queue (score = priority)
  + sliding-window rate limit (score = ts, range-query window)
  + delayed jobs (score = execute_at)
  + time-series index (score = timestamp)
```

### Q6. How does Redis Cluster shard data, and what are the limitations?
**Answer:** Redis Cluster shards by key using **hash slots** — there are 16,384 slots total, and each key is assigned to a slot via `CRC16(key) % 16384`. Each shard (node) owns a contiguous range of slots (e.g., node 1 owns slots 0-5460, node 2 owns 5461-10922, node 3 owns 10923-16383). The client computes the slot locally and routes directly to the owning node; on a `MOVED` redirect (slot moved during resharding), the client updates its cache and retries. **Hash tags** let you force multiple keys to the same slot by wrapping the tagged part in `{}`: `user:{42}:name` and `user:{42}:email` both hash to slot 19399 (only `42` is hashed), so they live on the same node and can be operated on together. Limitations: First, **multi-key operations must be in the same slot** — `MGET k1 k2` works only if k1 and k2 hash to the same slot (use hash tags). Second, **transactions (MULTI/EXEC) only work within a single slot** — cross-slot transactions are not supported. Third, **pub/sub broadcasts to all nodes** (in Redis 5 and earlier), which doesn't scale; Redis 7 added sharded pub/sub. Fourth, **resharding is online but slow** — moving slots between nodes re-streams data, takes minutes to hours for large datasets. Fifth, **no native cross-cluster joins or aggregations** — do those in the application. Sixth, **failover takes 10-30 seconds** (cluster consensus via gossip) — longer than Redis Sentinel's ~5-10s. Seventh, **minimum 6 nodes recommended** (3 masters + 3 replicas) for HA.
**Visual:**
```
Redis Cluster: 16384 hash slots, sharded across masters

  key -> CRC16(key) % 16384 -> slot -> owning master node

  Master 1: slots 0-5460      Master 2: slots 5461-10922   Master 3: slots 10923-16383
  +-----------+ replica       +-----------+ replica         +-----------+ replica
  |  shard 1  |<----          |  shard 2  |<----            |  shard 3  |<----
  +-----------+               +-----------+                 +-----------+

  Hash tags (force same slot):
    user:{42}:name  -> slot = CRC16("42") % 16384
    user:{42}:email -> same slot -> same node
    -> MGET user:{42}:name user:{42}:email  WORKS

  Limitations:
    + multi-key ops must share slot (use hash tags)
    + MULTI/EXEC only within single slot
    + sharded pub/sub only in Redis 7+
    + resharding is online but slow (slot migration)
    + failover: 10-30s (gossip consensus)
    + min 6 nodes (3 masters + 3 replicas) for HA

  vs DynamoDB: Amazon handles sharding invisibly (no slots visible)
  vs Memcached: client-side consistent hashing (no slots, no HA)
```

### Q7. What is the difference between write-through, write-behind, and cache-aside caching patterns?
**Answer:** **Cache-aside** (lazy loading): the application manages the cache explicitly — read cache first, on miss read DB and populate cache, on write invalidate (delete) the cache. Pros: cache only holds requested data (memory-efficient), cache failure degrades gracefully. Cons: stale data risk (write to DB without cache invalidation), stampede on cache miss, extra read-latency on first miss. **Write-through**: the application writes to the cache AND the database together (often via the cache as a proxy). Pros: cache is always consistent with DB (no stale reads), read latency is always cache-fast (no miss penalty after warmup). Cons: write latency is higher (two writes), cache holds data even if never read (memory waste), if cache crashes between writes you can have inconsistency. **Write-behind** (write-back): the application writes to the cache only, and the cache asynchronously flushes to the database (batched, delayed). Pros: write latency is cache-fast (sub-ms), writes are batched (DB load smoothed), survives brief DB outages. Cons: data loss risk if cache crashes before flush (use persistence: Redis AOF), reads see un-flushed data (usually fine since cache is source of truth short-term), complex to implement correctly (flush ordering, crash recovery). Real-world: cache-aside is the default (90% of deployments); write-through is used when reads must always be cache-fast (financial tickers); write-behind is used for high-write workloads where brief data loss is acceptable (view counters, analytics events).
**Visual:**
```
Cache-aside (lazy):
  read:  cache? hit : db -> cache -> return
  write: db -> cache.del(key)
  + memory efficient    + degrades gracefully
  - stale risk         - stampede on miss

Write-through:
  read:  cache (always warm) -> return
  write: cache + db (atomically)
  + always consistent   + read latency always fast
  - write latency (2x)  - cache holds unused data

Write-behind (write-back):
  read:  cache (source of truth) -> return
  write: cache only -> async flush to db (batched)
  + write latency fast  + batches DB load
  - data loss if cache crash before flush
  - complex (flush ordering, recovery)

When to use:
  default            -> cache-aside
  reads must be fast -> write-through
  writes are heavy   -> write-behind (accept some loss risk)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Twitter's home timeline reads happen on every app open (~300k req/sec for 200M users). They precompute timelines using Redis. Walk through the architecture and trade-offs.
**Answer:** Twitter uses **fan-out-on-write** with Redis as the timeline store. When a user tweets, the tweet is fanned out to all followers' timeline lists (Redis LIST or ZSET) — writing the tweet ID to each follower's `timeline:user:N` key. Reads are then trivial: `LRANGE timeline:user:42 0 50` returns the latest 50 tweet IDs in O(1)-ish, then hydrate the tweets themselves from a separate `tweet:ID` key (also Redis). This makes reads ~50ms p99 even at 300k req/sec, because the read is just a few Redis lookups (no computation, no DB hits). The trade-off: writes are expensive — a user with 10M followers writes 10M LIST pushes per tweet (the "celebrity problem"). Twitter mitigates this with a hybrid: for normal users, fan-out-on-write; for celebrities (millions of followers), fan-out-on-read (their tweets are fetched live and merged into the reader's timeline at read time). The architecture also needs: (1) Redis Cluster for sharding (200M timelines × ~800 tweets each = billions of entries, way more than one Redis instance); (2) persistence + replication (RDB + AOF, replicas for failover); (3) compaction (old tweets evicted from timelines beyond ~800 per user); (4) batching of fan-out writes (pipeline 1000 LPUSH commands at once). Real-world: Twitter runs massive Redis clusters (Twemproxy historically, now Redis Cluster) for exactly this — billions of ops/sec across the fleet.
**Visual:**
```
Twitter home timeline (fan-out-on-write + Redis):

  Alice tweets T1:
    fan-out to followers' timelines:
      LPUSH timeline:bob   T1   \
      LPUSH timeline:carol T1    }  1000s of LPUSHes per tweet
      LPUSH timeline:dave  T1   /   (batched via pipeline)

  Bob opens app:
    LRANGE timeline:bob 0 50   -> [T1, T_old, ...]   (fast: ~1ms)
    MGET tweet:T1 tweet:T_old  -> hydrate tweets      (fast: ~1ms)
    total p99 ~50ms

  Celebrity problem (10M followers):
    fan-out-on-write -> 10M LPUSHes per tweet (slow!)
    hybrid: celebrities use fan-out-on-read
            (fetch their tweets, merge into reader's timeline at read)

  Redis Cluster: shards timelines by user_id (hash tag {user:N})
  Persistence: RDB + AOF (timelines are rebuildable but expensive)
  Eviction: keep ~800 latest tweets per timeline
```

### Q2. You're building a real-time leaderboard for a mobile game with 10M players. Players score points constantly; the app shows the player's rank and top 10. How do you architect this with Redis?
**Answer:** Use Redis sorted sets (ZSETs). One ZSET per leaderboard: `ZADD leaderboard:global score player_id` for every score update, `ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global 0 9 WITHSCORES` for the top 10, `ZREVRANK leaderboard:global player_id` for the player's rank. For 10M players, ZSET operations are O(log N) ≈ 23 (log2 10M) — sub-millisecond. Atomic `ZINCRBY leaderboard:global 10 player_id` lets you increment scores atomically without read-modify-write races. Architecture: (1) Redis Cluster with the leaderboard key on a single shard (single ZSET, ~10M entries is fine — Redis handles 100M+ entries per ZSET); (2) replicas for read scaling (top-10 reads go to replicas, writes to primary); (3) persistence: RDB every 5 min + AOF for durability (so a crash doesn't lose the last 5 min of scores); (4) for daily/weekly leaderboards, use separate ZSETs (`leaderboard:daily:2024-01-15`) and a scheduled job to expire old ones; (5) for "your rank among friends," maintain per-friend-group ZSETs (updated on friend-add). Trade-offs: a single ZSET caps at one shard's throughput (~100k ZINCRBY/sec) — for higher write rates, shard by player_id hash and aggregate at read time, or use multiple leaderboard shards. Real-world: many game backends (and Reddit, Stack Overflow for reputation) use exactly this pattern; Redis ZSETs were designed for this use case.
**Visual:**
```
Redis ZSET leaderboard (10M players):

  ZADD leaderboard:global 1500 alice      \  atomic score update
  ZINCRBY leaderboard:global 10 alice     /  (no read-modify-write race)

  ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global 0 9 WITHSCORES  -> top 10  (O(log N + 10))
  ZREVRANK leaderboard:global alice            -> alice's rank (O(log N))

  For 10M players: log2(10M) ~ 23 ops -> sub-ms latency

Architecture:
  + Redis Cluster (1 shard for global LB, ~100k ZINCRBY/sec)
  + replicas for read scaling (top-10 reads -> replicas)
  + RDB every 5min + AOF (durability, lose <5min on crash)
  + daily/weekly LBs: separate ZSETs, scheduled expiry
  + friend-group LBs: per-group ZSET, updated on friend-add

Scaling beyond 100k writes/sec:
  + shard by player_id hash (LB1..LB16)
  + aggregate top-10 at read time (ZREVRANGE each, merge)
  + or use Redis 7 sharded pub/sub for cross-shard updates
```

### Q3. Stack Overflow has a 99.9% cache hit rate on Redis. Their DB is barely touched. What are the risks of this architecture, and how do they mitigate them?
**Answer:** A 99.9% cache hit rate means only 0.1% of reads hit the DB — extremely efficient, but it creates several risks. First, **the DB is a cold system** — when cache misses spike (cold start after deploy, cache corruption, popular cache key expiry), the DB gets 100-1000x its normal load and may crash. Mitigations: warm the cache before traffic shifts (preload hot keys), rate-limit DB queries (circuit breaker), keep DB capacity at 10x typical load. Second, **cache failure = full outage** — if Redis crashes, 100% of reads go to the DB, which can't handle it. Mitigations: Redis HA (replica + automatic failover, Redis Sentinel or Cluster), multi-AZ deployment, regular failover drills. Third, **stale data** — at 99.9% hit rate, cache entries live a long time, so invalidation must be correct. Stack Overflow invalidates on write (delete cache key after DB write), and uses short TTLs (5-60 min) as a safety net. Fourth, **cache stampede** — popular keys expiring simultaneously. Mitigations: probabilistic early expiration, jittered TTLs (TTL + random(0, 60s) so keys don't all expire at once). Fifth, **memory cost** — caching 99.9% of read data means a huge Redis footprint. Mitigations: LRU eviction (less-hot data falls out), periodic review of what's cached. Sixth, **operational complexity** — managing a giant Redis cluster (capacity, failover, monitoring) is non-trivial. Real-world: Stack Overflow runs ~5 Redis instances (each ~100GB), with careful monitoring of hit rate, memory, and latency.
**Visual:**
```
Stack Overflow: 99.9% cache hit rate

  App -> Redis (99.9% hit)  -> return
        \-> DB (0.1% miss)  -> populate Redis -> return

Risks + mitigations:
  1. DB is COLD (cache miss spike = DB crash)
     -> warm cache pre-deploy, rate-limit DB, 10x DB capacity
  2. CACHE FAILURE = full outage (100% load hits DB)
     -> Redis HA (replica + Sentinel failover), multi-AZ, drills
  3. STALE DATA (long-lived cache)
     -> invalidate on write + short TTL (5-60min) safety net
  4. STAMPEDE (popular key expiry)
     -> XFetch (early refresh) + jittered TTLs
  5. MEMORY COST (caching 99.9% of reads)
     -> LRU eviction, periodic cache audit
  6. OPS BURDEN (giant cluster)
     -> monitoring: hit rate, memory, latency, evictions

Real-world: ~5 Redis instances (~100GB each), 99.9% hit rate,
            DB barely touched, sub-50ms p99 page render
```

### Q4. You're building a rate limiter: 100 requests per user per minute, sliding window. How do you implement it with Redis?
**Answer:** The **sliding-window counter** approach using Redis: on each request, `INCR user:N:rl:window_key` where `window_key` is the current minute (e.g., `user:42:rl:202401151030`), and set TTL to 2x the window (120s) so old windows expire. To check the limit, sum the counters for the current and previous minute, weighted by the fraction of time remaining in the current minute: `count = curr_count + prev_count * (60 - sec_into_window) / 60`. If count <= 100, allow; else deny. This gives a smooth sliding window without storing every request timestamp. For stricter accuracy, use a **sorted set** approach: `ZADD user:N:rl:ts <timestamp> <request_id>` per request, `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE user:N:rl:ts 0 <now-60s>` to evict old entries, `ZCARD user:N:rl:ts` to get the count. O(log N) per request, more memory (one entry per request), but exact. For high scale, the counter approach is preferred (O(1), less memory). The pipeline: `INCR curr`, `EXPIRE curr 120`, `GET prev`, compute weighted sum, decide. Use Lua scripting to make it atomic (so concurrent requests don't race). Real-world: Stripe, GitHub, Twitter all use Redis-based rate limiting with this pattern. Trade-offs: counter approach is approximate (sliding window is granular per minute), sorted-set is exact but more memory; pick based on accuracy needs.
**Visual:**
```
Sliding-window rate limiter (100 req/user/min) with Redis:

Approach 1: Counter per minute (approximate, O(1))
  INCR user:42:rl:202401151030  -> 73  (current minute count)
  EXPIRE user:42:rl:202401151030 120
  GET  user:42:rl:202401151029  -> 95  (previous minute count)

  weighted = 73 + 95 * (60 - 30)/60 = 73 + 47.5 = 120.5
  -> 120.5 > 100, DENY

  Lua script: atomic INCR + EXPIRE + GET + decide

Approach 2: Sorted set (exact, O(log N), more memory)
  ZADD user:42:rl:ts 1705310580 req_id_1
  ZADD user:42:rl:ts 1705310581 req_id_2
  ZREMRANGEBYSCORE user:42:rl:ts 0 (now - 60)   # evict old
  count = ZCARD user:42:rl:ts                    # current window
  if count <= 100: allow else deny

Trade-offs:
  counter:    O(1), low memory, approximate (minute-granular)
  sorted set: O(log N), more memory, exact

Pipeline:    INCR curr -> EXPIRE curr -> GET prev -> decide (Lua atomic)
Real-world:  Stripe, GitHub, Twitter use Redis-based rate limiting
```

### Q5. A viral tweet causes one Redis key (the tweet's like count) to be accessed 1M times per second, overwhelming its owning shard. How do you mitigate hot keys?
**Answer:** Hot keys are a classic Redis scaling problem — a single key on one shard gets disproportionate traffic, capping throughput at that shard's limit (~100k ops/sec). Mitigations, in increasing order of complexity: First, **read replicas** — Redis Cluster lets you read from replicas (`READONLY` mode), so 5 replicas give 5x read throughput for the hot key. The catch: replica reads are eventually consistent (lag ~1ms), and writes still go to the primary — so this works for read-heavy hot keys, not write-heavy. Second, **client-side caching** (Redis 6 tracking) — clients cache hot key values locally and get invalidated by the server only when the key changes. For a like count that updates frequently, this helps less; for a hot config key that rarely changes, it's perfect. Third, **key splitting** — instead of `likes:tweet:42`, maintain `likes:tweet:42:0` through `likes:tweet:42:9` (10 keys), write to a random one on each like, sum all 10 on read. This spreads writes across 10 shards, giving 10x write throughput at the cost of 10 reads per count (still ~1ms total via pipeline). Fourth, **server-side Lua** — for atomic operations like INCR, run a Lua script on the primary so 1M INCRs/sec all happen in the primary's single thread (but this just confirms the bottleneck is the single thread, not the network). Fifth, **use a different store for viral data** — DynamoDB scales transparently for hot keys (Amazon handles the shard), or a CDN edge cache for read-only viral content. Real-world: Twitter handles viral tweets by combining read replicas + client-side caching + key splitting for the most extreme cases.

```
Mitigations (in increasing complexity):

1. READ REPLICAS (Redis Cluster READONLY)
   primary: writes (likes)
   replica1, replica2, ..., replica5: reads  -> 5x read throughput
   + simple, works for read-heavy hot keys
   - doesn't help write-heavy; eventual consistency (~1ms lag)

2. CLIENT-SIDE CACHING (Redis 6 tracking)
   client caches likes:tweet:42 locally
   server invalidates on change
   + zero network cost on hit
   - only helps if value rarely changes (not a counter)

3. KEY SPLITTING (write scaling)
   likes:tweet:42:0 ... likes:tweet:42:9  (10 keys, 10 shards)
   write: INCR random shard
   read:  MGET all 10, sum
   + 10x write throughput
   - 10 reads per count (pipelined, still fast)

4. SERVER-SIDE LUA (atomic INCR)

   + atomic, no race
   - confirms single-thread is the bottleneck

5. USE DYNAMODB OR CDN
   DynamoDB scales hot keys transparently (Amazon handles it)
   CDN edge cache for read-only viral content

Real-world: Twitter combines read replicas + client cache + key split
            for the most viral tweets
```

### Q6. You're using DynamoDB and notice your bill is $30k/month, mostly from a single GSI that's barely used. How do you diagnose and fix this?
**Answer:** DynamoDB charges per read/write capacity unit (RCU/WCU) for tables AND for each GSI — a GSI has its own capacity, sized independently of the base table. A common pitfall: a GSI is provisioned with high capacity "just in case," but is barely queried — you pay for the provisioned capacity whether or not you use it. Diagnosis: (1) Check CloudWatch metrics for each GSI — `ConsumedReadCapacityUnits`, `ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits`, `ProvisionedReadCapacityUnits`, `ProvisionedWriteCapacityUnits`. If provisioned >> consumed, you're overpaying. (2) Check the GSI's `ItemCount` and `SizeBytes` — if it's small but provisioned high, you're paying for capacity you don't need. (3) Check the GSI's `ThrottledRequests` — if zero, you have headroom to reduce. Fixes, in order of preference: (1) **Switch the GSI to on-demand capacity** — pay per actual request, no provisioning. Good for spiky or low-traffic GSIs. (2) **Reduce provisioned capacity** with autoscaling — set min low (e.g., 100 RCU) and max high (e.g., 10000 RCU); DynamoDB scales within 5 minutes. (3) **Drop the GSI entirely** if it's barely used — query the base table with a scan instead (slower but no GSI cost), or move the query to OpenSearch if you need flexible search. (4) **Compress the GSI** — if the GSI projects all attributes, project only keys (`KEYS_ONLY`) or specific attributes (`INCLUDE`) to reduce storage and write amplification. (5) **Consider sparse indexes** — only index rows where the indexed attribute exists (omit nulls), reducing GSI size. Real-world: many teams cut DynamoDB bills 50-80% by auditing GSIs.
**Visual:**
```
DynamoDB GSI cost trap:

  Table:  users (PK: user_id, SK: none)
    provisioned: 10000 RCU / 5000 WCU   (right-sized)
  GSI:    users_by_email (email -> user_id)
    provisioned: 5000 RCU / 2000 WCU    (barely queried!)

  Bill: table $5k + GSI $25k = $30k/month (GSI dominates)

Diagnosis (CloudWatch metrics):
  ConsumedReadCapacityUnits (GSI)  = 50   (vs 5000 provisioned)
  ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits (GSI) = 200  (vs 2000 provisioned)
  ThrottledRequests (GSI)          = 0    (headroom available)
  -> overprovisioned 100x

Fixes (in preference order):
  1. Switch GSI to on-demand (pay per request, no provisioning)
  2. Reduce provisioned + autoscaling (min 100, max 10000)
  3. Drop GSI entirely (use Scan or OpenSearch instead)
  4. Compress projection (ALL -> KEYS_ONLY or INCLUDE specific)
  5. Sparse index (only index non-null emails)

Real-world: GSI audit typically saves 50-80% on DynamoDB bills
```

### Q7. Your team stores user sessions in sticky-session cookies (encrypted in the browser). As you scale to 100 servers, you're considering moving sessions to Redis. What changes, and what are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** Moving from sticky-session cookies to Redis-backed sessions is a common scaling step. **Current state**: each app server stores sessions locally (in-memory or file), and a load balancer uses a session cookie to route subsequent requests to the same server (sticky sessions). Problem: adding/removing servers disrupts sessions, server crashes lose sessions, and load balancing is uneven (sticky sessions ignore actual server load). **Redis-backed sessions**: each session is stored in Redis with the session ID as the key (`session:<id>` -> user data, TTL = session timeout). Any app server can read/write any session — load balancing becomes truly round-robin (or least-connections), server crashes don't lose sessions (Redis is the source of truth), and adding servers is trivial. Trade-offs: (1) **Added latency** — every request does a Redis GET (~1ms) instead of local memory (~10µs), adding ~1ms to every request. Usually acceptable. (2) **Redis becomes critical infrastructure** — if Redis crashes, all sessions are lost (users logged out). Mitigations: Redis HA (replica + Sentinel/Cluster failover), persistence (AOF), session re-creation flow. (3) **Redis capacity** — sessions are small (~1KB each), but at 100M active sessions that's 100GB. Plan capacity. (4) **Connection pool** — each app server needs a Redis connection pool (e.g., 50 connections), so 100 servers × 50 = 5000 connections to Redis — Redis handles this fine but monitor. (5) **TTL management** — set TTL on every session key (`EXPIRE session:<id> 1800`) so inactive sessions auto-expire. Real-world: GitHub, Twitter, Instagram all use Redis for sessions for exactly these reasons.
**Visual:**
```
Sticky-session cookies (BEFORE):
  Browser --cookie ABC--> LB --route to server 3--> Server 3 (session ABC)
  (server 3 must handle all ABC requests; LB ignores actual load)

  + simple, no shared state
  - server crash = session lost
  - add/remove server = some sessions disrupted
  - uneven load balancing

Redis-backed sessions (AFTER):
  Browser --cookie ABC--> LB --any server--> Server N
                                          \-> GET session:ABC from Redis
                                          \-> handle request
                                          \-> SET session:ABC (update TTL)

  + true round-robin LB (any server handles any session)
  + server crash doesn't lose session (Redis = source of truth)
  + add/remove servers freely
  - +1ms latency per request (Redis GET)
  - Redis is critical (HA + persistence required)
  - capacity planning (100GB for 100M sessions)
  - connection pool (5000 conns to Redis across 100 servers)

Real-world: GitHub, Twitter, Instagram all use Redis for sessions
```
